key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Wilson
key_cases.holding: The court held that a parent facing an intervention petition and entry on the Central Registry has a protected liberty interest and a due process right of confrontation, and that allowing the child to testify outside his presence without an individualized finding of trauma violated that right.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling South Carolina authority on the due process owed before a substantiated finding places a person on the Central Registry.
key_cases.quote: Because Wilson did not have the opportunity to be heard in a meaningful manner, his due process right was violated.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Jennifer M.
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the finding of abuse and neglect and the order placing the mother on the Central Registry, holding she could not be found to have abused an unborn child by conduct occurring while she neither knew nor had reason to know she was pregnant, and that the drug-test evidence was inadmissible hearsay without foundation.
key_cases.relevance: It shows that a substantiated finding and Central Registry entry must rest on properly admitted evidence and a culpable mental state.
key_cases.quote: the family court erred in finding Mother abused and neglected her unborn Child based upon conduct occurring while Mother did not know or have reason to know she was pregnant

key_cases.case_name: Wardlaw v. S.C. Dep't of Soc. Servs.
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding the family court had subject matter jurisdiction, that an eighty-two day wait for an administrative hearing was not the 'expedited review' S.C. Code § 63-7-1230 requires, and that ordering the name removed from the Registry pending that hearing was a proper remedy.
key_cases.relevance: Wardlaw is the controlling authority on the timeliness of the administrative review that follows an early Central Registry entry.
key_cases.quote: we find no error by the family court in concluding eighty-two days is not expedited as contemplated by the statute

key_cases.holding: The court held that 'child' in South Carolina's child abuse and endangerment statute includes a viable fetus, so a mother's prenatal drug use can constitute criminal child neglect, and found no due process violation.
key_cases.relevance: Whitner supplies the substantive definition of 'child' that underpins a substantiated finding based on prenatal conduct.
key_cases.quote: We hold the word "child" as used in that statute includes viable fetuses.

key_cases.case_name: Richland County Department of Social Services v. Earles
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that unavailability based on severe emotional trauma requires a finding that the child would be traumatized by testifying in person, by videotaped deposition and by closed-circuit television, that the record here supported that finding, and that clear and convincing evidence showed the home could not be made safe.
key_cases.relevance: Earles shows how the individualized trauma finding Wilson requires is actually made and what expert proof will sustain a child's out-of-court statements as the basis for a founded finding.
key_cases.quote: Unavailability under § 19-1-180(B)(2)(a)(v) requires a finding that the child will suffer severe trauma by testifying under all three methods.

key_cases.case_name: Joubert v. South Carolina Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for DSS, holding that a damages action arising from an 'indicated' institutional neglect finding and Central Registry listing is governed by the Tort Claims Act and that, absent a verified claim, the two-year limitations period applied and had expired before suit was filed.
key_cases.relevance: Joubert traces the entire track that follows an 'indicated' finding and Central Registry entry — administrative fair hearing, family court review under former § 20-7-655, expungement — and then holds that any damages claim over the erroneous finding is time-barred under the Tort Claims Act unless a verified claim was filed.
key_cases.quote: if a plaintiff files a statutorily-defined claim within one year of the loss or injury, the statute of limitations is extended to three years
